retrieved.text: A transparency record is not a mandate. It does not grant a power to deny a benefit, and it does not replace an explanation to the person who was refused. It tells the public that the tool exists and how a human remains in the decision.
Informing clients of recourse options to challenge the administrative decision. Ensuring that recourse options are timely, effective, and easy to access.

Providing a meaningful explanation to clients of how and why the decision was made. For a decision that results in the denial of a benefit or service, a more detailed plain-language explanation is provided to the client, including the principal factors that led to the output and how that output was used by human officers. Explanations must also inform clients of relevant recourse options.

The global lesson is domain-level. An assistant that denies a benefit or asserts a debt needs a cited legal basis, an explanation a person can use, and a human review path that can stop the decision. Publishing a model card after the fact does not supply that path.

Ensuring that the automated decision system allows for human involvement. At higher impact levels the final decision must be made by a human. Decisions cannot be made without having clearly defined human involvement during the decision-making process. Humans review the decisions or recommendations made by the system for accuracy and appropriateness and can intervene.

The memorandum expects a human fallback when the system fails or when a person asks for review of a rights-impacting decision. An outage of a vendor-hosted model does not suspend that duty. The agency still needs a way to continue the service and to report the incident. Data processed in a foreign vendor region remains subject to the agency's residency and privacy review.

The objective of this directive is to ensure that automated decision systems are used in a manner that reduces risks to clients, departments and Canadian society, and leads to more efficient, accurate, consistent and interpretable decisions made pursuant to Canadian law. Decisions made by departments are to be data-driven and responsible, and comply with procedural fairness and due process requirements.

Operate a reliable service. When the digital channel fails, users still need to complete the task. Reliability includes a staffed fallback and a published account of performance, not only an uptime figure for the model host.

retrieved.text: Make sure the service works with the most common assistive technologies, screen readers or speech recognition software for example, and test the service with disabled users and with older users. Meet level AA of the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines as a minimum. Think about accessibility from the start, including people who use a dialect or a language other than the one the model was tuned on.

Work towards creating a service that solves a whole problem for users, working with other teams and organisations where necessary. Design and develop your service around the needs of users, not around technologies or pre-selected solutions. This includes generative artificial intelligence and commercial off-the-shelf products. Users should not have to understand how government works in order to use public services.

The global lesson is domain-level. An assistant that denies a benefit or asserts a debt needs a cited legal basis, an explanation a person can use, and a human review path that can stop the decision. Publishing a model card after the fact does not supply that path.

Provide a joined up experience across all channels. Test all the parts of the service that the user interacts with, online parts and offline parts like letters. A person who cannot finish in the automated channel still needs a consistent route through the staffed channel.

Build a service that is simple, intuitive and comprehensible. And test it with users to make sure it works for them. Make sure the service helps the user to do the thing they need to do as simply as possible, so that people succeed first time, with the minimum of help.

The Framework Convention requires parties to address risks to human rights, democracy and the rule of law across the lifecycle of an AI system. For a public-service assistant that denies a benefit, that means a remedy a person can actually use, not only an internal log. Transparency and accountability are duties of the deployer, including when a vendor hosts the model.

AI Readiness 2.0 dimension D7 Strategy Alignment. Describes the overall gains of coordination for AI integration strategies across distributed entities including stakeholders and domains. Mapped factors: Standards. Example metrics: Coordination Level; Time to Go-Live; Intent Representations; Interoperability Standards; Service Provider Mapping; Domain Impact.

Providing a meaningful explanation to clients of how and why the decision was made. For a decision that results in the denial of a benefit or service, a more detailed plain-language explanation is provided to the client, including the principal factors that led to the output and how that output was used by human officers. Explanations must also inform clients of relevant recourse options.

The UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI calls for inclusive access and non-discrimination in the design of public AI services. A public assistant that answers only in one standard language, or that cannot be used with a screen reader, fails that inclusion principle even when the underlying model is accurate for other users. Member states are encouraged to promote linguistic diversity and to assess impacts on persons with disabilities.

The Recommendation ties AI in public services to proportionality, safety, and human oversight. An automated denial of a social benefit is the kind of decision the Recommendation expects a person to be able to understand and to challenge. The briefing does not restate country-specific obligations.
The Recommendation was adopted by UNESCO in 2021. URL: https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000381137 The official text is not reproduced. This briefing is original and is licensed CC0.

AI Readiness 2.0 dimension D6 Human Interface. Measures the use of AI for ease of human interaction with systems/workflows across various devices. Mapped factors: Standards, Deployment Support. Example metrics: AI-Ready Interface Penetration; Local Language Models; Interaction Channels; Usability Level; Cultural Sensitivity; Safety Integration.

AI Readiness 2.0 dimension D2 Generated Content Marketplace. Measures the ease of creation of new services using AI, including new datasets/models generated for new AI services. Mapped factors: Data, Open Source and Code. Example metrics: Ecosystem Parameters; Guardrails; Multi-modal Support; Fake Detection; Regional Customization.

EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689) - Summary 1. OVERVIEW The EU AI Act is the first comprehensive legal framework on AI worldwide. It entered into force on 1 August 2024 and will be fully applicable by 2 August 2026, with phased implementation. 2. RISK-BASED CLASSIFICATION The Act classifies AI systems into four risk tiers: a) Unacceptable Risk (Prohibited): Social scoring by governments, real-time biometric identification in public spaces (with exceptions), manipulation techniques, exploitation of vulnerabilities. Effective from Feb 2025. b) High Risk: AI in critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential services, law enforcement, migration, justice. Requires conformity assessments, risk management, data governance, transparency, human oversight. c) Limited Risk: Chatbots, deepfakes, emotion recognition. Must meet transparency obligations (users must know they interact with AI). d) Minimal Risk: Spam filters, AI in video games. No specific obligations. 3. GENERAL PURPOSE AI (GPAI) MODELS - All GPAI providers must provide technical documentation, comply with copyright law, publish training data summaries - Systemic risk GPAI (>10^25 FLOPs training compute): additional obligations including model evaluations, adversarial testing, incident reporting, cybersecurity measures 4. IMPLEMENTATION TIMELINE - Feb 2025: Prohibited practices and AI literacy in force - Aug 2025: GPAI model obligations in force - Aug 2026: Full application (high-risk AI in regulated products) - Aug 2027: Extended transition for some high-risk systems 5. GOVERNANCE STRUCTURE - European AI Office (within European Commission) - National competent authorities in each EU member state - AI Board (representatives from member states) - Advisory forum and scientific panel 6. PENALTIES - Up to 35M EUR or 7% of global turnover for prohibited AI practices - Up to 15M EUR or 3% for high-risk non-compliance - Up to 7.5M EUR or 1.5% for incorrect information 7. RELEVANCE TO ITU AI READINESS FRAMEWORK - Dimension 10 (AI & Policies): The most comprehensive regulatory framework globally; benchmark for policy evaluation - Dimension 7 (Strategy Alignment): EU-wide coordination mechanism - Dimension 5 (AI Integration): Compliance requirements affect how AI is integrated in workflows - Dimension 1 (Data Marketplace): Data governance requirements for high-risk AI - Dimension 6 (Human Interface): Transparency requirements for AI-human interaction - Provides a model for developing countries designing AI governance frameworks
